transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Williams, hello. I'm Dr. Aris, one of the residents on the surgical team. I wanted to come in and talk to you about the blood transfusion you received during your surgery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The nurse already told me something happened. She said it wasn't the right blood.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you've already had a conversation about this, but I wanted to be the one to explain it to you directly. I'm sorry for any confusion that's been caused so far. We were really busy in the unit yesterday and the pre-operative blood type verification was skipped.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Skipped? How do you just skip that? I'm lying there and you're just... you didn't check?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're right, we didn't. It was a failure in our protocol. Because of that, you received a compatible blood type, but not the ideal one for your specific match.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't believe this. I can't even be here. My kids are at home with my sister and she can't do this for long. I'm already terrified about when I can go back to work, and now you're telling me you messed up my blood?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you're feeling completely overwhelmed, not just with what happened here, but with everything waiting for you at home with your children. I can only imagine how frightening it is to feel like your recovery is being put at risk while you're already worrying about your two jobs.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I can't afford to have a complication. If I stay here longer than I have to, I don't know what I'm going to do. Was the blood poisonous or something? Do I have a reaction?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let me explain the clinical side. When we say it wasn't the ideal match, it means it was a different group that the body generally accepts, but it's not the perfect one. It's not poisonous, but it can sometimes cause a mild reaction.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So am I okay right now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are monitoring your vitals. I just need to quickly check your chart for the latest labs—actually, looking at these, your white cell count is stable. We just need to keep an eye on you for the next twenty-four hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What if I'm not okay? What if this ruins my recovery?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is scary. I want you to know that I am here to make sure we handle this correctly moving forward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Who is going to make sure it doesn't happen again? Because "we were busy" isn't a good enough reason to gamble with my life.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're absolutely right. Being busy is no excuse for skipping a safety check. I realize that doesn't take away the fear you're feeling right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, it doesn't. I just want to go home to my kids.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear that. Your kids are your priority, and getting you back to them safely is ours too. Regarding the plan, we'll do another blood draw tomorrow morning to monitor for any antibodies.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Once those results come back, we can determine if we need any further treatment. We'll keep you updated on those results by tomorrow afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do I have to do? Do I just lay here?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: All I need from you is to let us know immediately if you feel any itching or shortness of breath. Just press the call button if anything feels off.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just can't believe this happened.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. It's a lot to take in. I'll go check in with the attending physician and I'll be back in a bit.

H.justification: The resident allows the patient to finish their turns and remains regulated under pushback, with no interruptions or rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and lay language was used, but the resident never checked for the patient's comprehension of the explanation.

A.justification: While a direct apology was used, it was immediately diluted by an excuse ('We were really busy in the unit yesterday').

R.justification: The resident named specific emotions ('overwhelmed', 'frightening', 'fear') and referenced specific patient content regarding her children and jobs.

T.justification: The resident provided specific steps (blood draw), timelines (tomorrow morning/afternoon), the patient's role (report itching/shortness of breath), and addressed prevention by admitting the safety check was skipped.
